# Methods {#sec-methods}

> To empirically examine whether adaptation discourse reflects epistemological control, I develop a mixed methods approach that combines computational text analysis with auto-ethnographic reflection, enabling analysis of both the structural patterns and cultural processes that shape expert knowledge production.

This research addresses questions about epistemological control and expert authority that require methodological innovation beyond traditional single-method approaches. Examining whether expert systems produce genuine knowledge diversity or systematic convergence demands both systematic analysis of expert discourse across contexts and critical understanding of how this discourse is produced within expert cultures. The methodology therefore integrates computational analysis of National Adaptation Plans with reflexive analysis of my own positioning within expert governance systems, using climate adaptation as the empirical case for testing broader theories of control.

The mixed methods design reflects both practical and theoretical considerations. Practically, examining epistemological control requires analysis across multiple scales—from individual expert socialization to institutional discourse patterns to global knowledge convergence. Theoretically, understanding how control operates through expert systems requires insight into both the structural outcomes (discourse homogenization) and the cultural processes (expert reproduction) that produce these outcomes. Neither computational nor ethnographic analysis alone could adequately address questions about how expert authority operates as both knowledge system and cultural reproduction.

My sustained engagement with climate governance provides unique analytical access to expert cultures while raising important methodological and ethical questions about studying systems from within. Rather than treating this insider positioning as limitation requiring control, I employ auto-ethnographic methods that use reflexive analysis as analytical resource. This approach enables examination of how expert systems shape both policy outputs and expert subjectivities, revealing connections between institutional patterns and individual experiences of expert socialization within systems of control.

The chapter proceeds through three methodological discussions. First, I detail the computational text analysis approach, explaining how structural topic modeling and the Control Index enable systematic examination of discourse convergence patterns across expert-produced policy documents. Then I examine the auto-ethnographic component, discussing how my trajectory through expert systems provides analytical insight into how epistemological control operates through cultural reproduction. Finally, I address the integration of these approaches, explaining how mixed methods analysis enables examination of expert governance as both structural discourse and lived cultural practice.

This methodological combination serves the broader theoretical project of understanding how expert systems operate as mechanisms of epistemological control. The computational analysis reveals the homogenization that characterizes expert knowledge production, while auto-ethnographic analysis illuminates how expert cultures reproduce the assumptions and practices that generate this homogenization. Together, these approaches enable analysis of climate adaptation not just as policy framework but as exemplar of how expert authority shapes whose knowledge counts and which futures are imaginable. Climate adaptation becomes the empirical window through which broader patterns of expert control can be examined and understood.

# Computational Text Analysis

The proliferation of digital policy documents presents both an opportunity and a methodological challenge for social research. While the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) repository contains hundreds of adaptation planning documents representing diverse geographical contexts and epistemological traditions, traditional qualitative methods struggle to systematically analyze such volumes of text while maintaining analytical depth. Computational text analysis emerges as a crucial bridge between the richness of interpretive analysis and the scale required for examining global policy discourse.

This methodological approach proves particularly valuable when investigating questions of epistemological convergence and diversity in international governance. The National Adaptation Plans, submitted by 47 countries ranging from small island states to landlocked nations, constitute a corpus that would require months or years of manual coding to analyze comprehensively. Yet these documents contain critical insights into how climate adaptation is understood, framed, and operationalized across radically different contexts. Computational methods allow researchers to identify patterns of discourse concentration while preserving the ability to interrogate specific textual instances that illuminate broader trends.

The application of computational text analysis to policy documents represents a significant departure from its origins in information retrieval and computational linguistics. Where early applications focused primarily on classification tasks and sentiment analysis, contemporary approaches enable researchers to examine the subtle ways in which policy language constructs particular versions of reality. This shift aligns with critical discourse analysis traditions that understand language not merely as description but as constitutive of social and political relations [@mullet2018]. In the context of climate adaptation planning, this means examining not just what topics appear in NAPs, but how their prevalence and distribution might indicate systematic patterns of knowledge production and epistemological control.

Structural topic modeling, as one specific computational approach, offers unique advantages for analyzing policy discourse. Unlike simple word frequency analysis or keyword extraction, topic models identify latent semantic structures that capture how concepts cluster together in practice [@roberts2016]. This capability proves essential when examining whether apparent diversity in adaptation planning masks underlying homogenization. A country may use distinct vocabulary while reproducing identical conceptual frameworks—a pattern that would be invisible to surface-level analysis but emerges clearly through topic modeling's probabilistic approach to semantic relationships.

The methodological power of computational text analysis extends beyond pattern identification to hypothesis testing about the factors shaping discourse. By incorporating document-level metadata—such as geographic region, income classification, or climate vulnerability indicators—researchers can statistically examine which characteristics most strongly influence how adaptation is discussed [@roberts2019]. This capacity transforms descriptive observations about textual similarity into testable claims about the mechanisms producing convergence or divergence in global policy discourse. Such analysis becomes particularly relevant when investigating whether adaptation planning reflects genuine knowledge transfer or represents what critical scholars term epistemicide—the systematic elimination of alternative ways of knowing [@dejong2025].

Recent applications demonstrate how computational text analysis can illuminate power dynamics embedded in institutional discourse. Studies of World Bank and OECD documents reveal how seemingly neutral technical language systematically frames governance challenges in ways that preclude certain political possibilities [@defrancesco2020]. Similarly, analysis of urban climate action plans uncovers striking homogenization despite radically different urban contexts, suggesting that policy mobility operates through discourse standardization rather than substantive knowledge exchange [@westman2023]. These findings underscore how computational methods can operationalize critical theoretical insights about the relationship between language, knowledge, and power in global governance.

The integration of computational and interpretive approaches addresses longstanding tensions in discourse analysis between systematic comparison and contextual sensitivity. Traditional critical discourse analysis excels at unpacking the ideological work performed by specific texts but struggles to make claims about broader patterns across large corpora [@jacobs2019]. Conversely, purely quantitative content analysis may identify patterns but miss the nuanced ways language performs political work. Computational text analysis, particularly when combined with careful qualitative interpretation, enables what @jacobs2019 term "distant reading" that maintains connection to close textual analysis. Researchers can zoom out to identify corpus-wide patterns, then zoom in to examine how specific documents exemplify or deviate from these trends.

For climate adaptation research specifically, computational text analysis offers crucial insights into how global frameworks interact with local knowledge systems. The technical apparatus of adaptation planning—vulnerability assessments, risk matrices, implementation frameworks—creates a standardized vocabulary that may overshadow indigenous and place-based understandings of environmental change. By systematically analyzing how different countries deploy this vocabulary, researchers can identify whether adaptation planning operates as what @ferguson1994 termed an "anti-politics machine" that transforms political questions into technical problems. The computational approach makes visible patterns of depoliticization that might otherwise remain hidden within the sheer volume of planning documents.

The temporal dimension of policy discourse also becomes accessible through computational methods. As countries update and revise their NAPs, text analysis can track how adaptation framings evolve in response to changing political priorities, scientific understanding, or institutional pressures. This longitudinal perspective reveals whether initial diversity in approaches converges over time toward standardized models, suggesting the operation of what institutional theorists identify as isomorphic pressures in global governance. Such analysis provides empirical grounding for theoretical debates about path dependency and institutional learning in international environmental regimes.

Beyond identifying what is present in texts, computational analysis excels at revealing systematic absences—the concepts, relationships, and possibilities that remain unspoken across hundreds of pages of planning documents. These silences often prove as politically significant as explicit statements, indicating the boundaries of acceptable discourse within institutional settings. When certain topics consistently appear together while others remain systematically separated, these patterns suggest underlying assumptions about causality, responsibility, and possibility that shape how problems are understood and solutions imagined. In adaptation planning, the presence or absence of terms related to historical responsibility, climate justice, or systemic transformation becomes analytically tractable through computational methods.

The scalability of computational text analysis also enables comparative research designs that would be practically impossible through traditional methods. Researchers can examine whether patterns identified in one policy domain—such as the homogenization of urban climate planning—appear across other areas of environmental governance. This capacity for systematic comparison across contexts, time periods, and institutional settings transforms isolated observations into generalizable insights about how global governance operates through discourse standardization. Such comparisons become particularly valuable for understanding whether the convergence observed in adaptation planning represents a unique phenomenon or exemplifies broader trends in international development and environmental management.

However, the application of computational methods to policy texts requires careful attention to the specificities of bureaucratic language. Policy documents employ specialized vocabularies, complex grammatical structures, and intertextual references that standard natural language processing tools may not handle appropriately. The preprocessing decisions—how to handle acronyms, whether to preserve bureaucratic phrasings, how to treat citations to other documents—significantly influence what patterns become visible through analysis. These choices constitute interpretive acts that shape findings as fundamentally as decisions about which documents to include or how to specify topic models.

The validation of computational findings against qualitative knowledge remains essential for meaningful interpretation. While algorithms can identify that certain terms cluster together statistically, understanding what this clustering means for policy and practice requires deep contextual knowledge. A topic combining "vulnerability," "assessment," and "participatory" might indicate genuine attention to community engagement or merely reflect the ritualistic adoption of required terminology. Distinguishing between these possibilities demands combining computational patterns with careful reading of exemplar texts and understanding of institutional contexts. This integration ensures that computational efficiency does not come at the cost of interpretive validity.

Furthermore, computational text analysis provides tools for examining how technical language performs boundary work in global governance. The specialized vocabulary of adaptation planning—terms like "mainstreaming," "resilience," "adaptive capacity"—creates barriers to participation while claiming universal applicability. By mapping how this technical language proliferates across different national contexts, researchers can examine whether capacity building and knowledge transfer actually build local capacity or primarily train local actors to speak institutional languages. This analysis becomes crucial for understanding whether adaptation planning enables diverse responses to climate change or operates as a mechanism of epistemological standardization.

The methodological transparency afforded by computational approaches also addresses concerns about reproducibility in qualitative research. While interpretive analysis necessarily involves subjective judgment, computational text analysis requires explicit documentation of data processing, model specification, and analytical choices. This transparency enables other researchers to verify findings, test alternative specifications, and build cumulative knowledge about discourse patterns. Such reproducibility becomes particularly important when research aims to influence policy debates, as findings can be scrutinized and validated independently of researchers' theoretical commitments.

Ultimately, computational text analysis serves not as a replacement for critical interpretation but as a powerful tool for systematic critique. By making visible the patterns through which global governance operates—the convergences that suggest control, the divergences that indicate possibility, the silences that reveal power—these methods provide empirical grounding for theoretical arguments about knowledge, power, and justice in climate adaptation. The ability to analyze hundreds of documents while maintaining analytical depth enables researchers to move beyond anecdotal observations toward systematic understanding of how adaptation planning shapes possibilities for responding to climate change. This combination of scale and specificity, pattern and particularity, makes computational text analysis indispensable for understanding whether global climate governance enables diverse pathways toward climate justice or operates as a mechanism of epistemological control.

## Structural Topic Modeling

```{r
# Load data from JSON files for inline references
process_dfm <- jsonlite::read_json("../data/process_dfm.json")
fit_model <- jsonlite::read_json("../data/fit_model.json")
name_topics <- jsonlite::read_json("../data/name_topics.json")
calculate_metrics <- jsonlite::read_json("../data/calculate_metrics.json")

# Formatting functions
pct <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(round(x * 100, digits), "%")
num <- function(x) {
  if (x < 10000) {
    return(as.character(round(x)))
  } else {
    return(format(round(x), big.mark = ","))
  }
}

# Document processing parameters
n_documents <- process_dfm$metadata$input_documents
n_tokens <- num(process_dfm$metadata$input_tokens)
n_vocabulary <- num(process_dfm$metadata$input_vocabulary)
n_segments <- process_dfm$metadata$segmentation$segment_count
n_final_docs <- process_dfm$metadata$final_documents
n_final_vocab <- num(process_dfm$metadata$final_vocabulary)
n_final_tokens <- num(process_dfm$metadata$final_tokens)
avg_segment_length <- num(process_dfm$metadata$segmentation$avg_segment_length)
n_custom_stopwords <- process_dfm$metadata$custom_stopwords_count

# Thresholds (as percentages)
min_doc_threshold <- pct(0.1)  # From process_dfm.R default
max_doc_threshold <- pct(0.8)  # From process_dfm.R default
min_docs_absolute <- process_dfm$metadata$min_docs_absolute
max_docs_absolute <- process_dfm$metadata$max_docs_absolute

# Model parameters
k_topics <- fit_model$metadata$k
n_iterations <- 200  # From fit_model.R default
coherence_mean <- round(fit_model$metadata$semantic_coherence_mean, 1)
exclusivity_mean <- round(fit_model$metadata$exclusivity_mean, 1)

# Statistical testing
n_categories <- 3  # Income, Region, Geography
n_subcategories <- 16  # From calculate_metrics results
n_significant <- sum(calculate_metrics$data$results$significant, na.rm = TRUE)
min_effect <- round(min(calculate_metrics$data$results$effect_size, na.rm = TRUE), 3)
max_effect <- round(max(calculate_metrics$data$results$effect_size, na.rm = TRUE), 3)
```

The implementation of structural topic modeling for this analysis required navigating multiple methodological trade-offs between computational feasibility, interpretative clarity, and statistical rigor. Unlike standard applications of topic modeling to homogeneous corpora, analyzing National Adaptation Plans presented unique challenges: documents varied dramatically in length from under 5,000 to over 100,000 words, were extracted from often poorly-scanned PDFs submitted by ministries across the developing world, combined technical climate science with bureaucratic planning language, and represented fundamentally different institutional contexts despite superficial similarity. These characteristics—both technical and substantive—demanded specific preprocessing decisions and analytical innovations that shaped both what patterns could be detected and how they should be interpreted.

The analytical pipeline proceeded through five integrated stages, each involving critical decisions about how to balance competing methodological priorities. Document preprocessing addressed the challenge of making heterogeneous policy documents computationally comparable while preserving meaningful variation. The segmentation strategy resolved the technical problem of documents with radically different lengths biasing topic distributions. Model specification incorporated document metadata as covariates to test hypotheses about institutional influence on discourse patterns. Topic interpretation combined algorithmic metrics with substantive knowledge to identify meaningful thematic categories. Finally, the development of the Control Index provided a novel measure for quantifying discourse concentration patterns that standard topic modeling metrics cannot capture.

The preprocessing pipeline began by standardizing the `r n_documents` English-language NAPs into comparable analytical units. Initial processing retained documents containing `r n_tokens` tokens representing a vocabulary of `r n_vocabulary` unique terms. Standard text preprocessing steps—lowercasing, punctuation removal, and number removal—were applied uniformly [@stm], but several domain-specific decisions proved critical. Geographic stopwords were systematically removed using the countrycode package [@countrycode] to extract country names and demonyms, preventing the emergence of topics defined purely by national identifiers rather than substantive content. This removed `r n_custom_stopwords` geographic terms that would have dominated topic distributions given the documents' frequent self-references.

The decision to apply stemming using Porter's algorithm collapsed morphological variants (e.g., "adapt," "adaptation," "adapting" → "adapt"), substantially reducing vocabulary while preserving semantic relationships. This choice prioritized thematic coherence over lexical precision, accepting that some meaning distinctions would be lost (e.g., "adaptation" versus "adaptive" collapsed to "adapt") in exchange for more robust topic identification. Minimum word length was set at three characters, and terms appearing in fewer than `r min_doc_threshold` or more than `r max_doc_threshold` of documents were excluded, eliminating both rare technical terms and ubiquitous climate vocabulary that provided no discriminatory power.

The most significant preprocessing decision involved document segmentation to address the radical length disparities. With document lengths ranging from 4,827 to 112,453 tokens, the standard assumption that document length reflects topic diversity rather than institutional verbosity was untenable. The segmentation algorithm targeted approximately `r n_segments` segments across the corpus, calculating optimal segment length dynamically based on total tokens. Documents shorter than 50 words remained intact, while longer documents were split at approximately `r avg_segment_length`-word intervals, creating `r n_segments` analytical segments that preserved document membership through metadata while enabling fair topic allocation across countries regardless of their plans' length. This approach meant that Tonga's concise 12-page plan received similar analytical weight to Sudan's 234-page document, preventing length from becoming a confounding variable in topic prevalence estimates.

The structural topic model was specified with K=`r k_topics` topics based on systematic evaluation of model fit across K∈{5,6,7,8,9,10,12,15} using semantic coherence and exclusivity metrics [@mimno2011; @roberts2019]. The eight-topic solution maximized the coherence-exclusivity frontier, achieving mean semantic coherence of `r coherence_mean` and mean exclusivity of `r exclusivity_mean`. Lower K values produced overly broad topics that obscured important distinctions between sectoral and procedural content, while higher K values generated redundant splits within conceptually unified themes without improving interpretability.

The STM specification incorporated document-level covariates through the prevalence formula to test hypotheses about institutional influence on topic distributions. Three categorization schemes were implemented as covariates: World Bank income classifications (4 levels: low, lower-middle, upper-middle, high), UN regional groupings (6 regions), and climate vulnerability categories (SIDS, LLDC, Other). This specification allowed the model to estimate how topic prevalence varied systematically across these institutional categories while accounting for their correlations. Model estimation employed variational expectation-maximization with `r n_iterations` iterations [@stm], using spectral initialization for stability across runs. Post-estimation, segment-level topic proportions were aggregated back to document level by averaging across segments belonging to each original document, weighted by segment length to preserve the influence of longer passages while preventing single lengthy sections from dominating topic assignments.

Topic interpretation combined multiple identification strategies to ensure robust labeling beyond subjective interpretation. The FREX (frequency-exclusivity) metric [@roberts2016] identified terms that were both common within topics and distinctive across them, providing the primary basis for interpretation. For each topic, the top 10 FREX terms were extracted, revealing clear thematic clusters. Topics were then manually named by selecting the most representative FREX term and unstemming it to create interpretable labels that reflected the topic's substantive content.

Topic validation proceeded through three approaches. First, examining the highest-probability documents for each topic confirmed that FREX terms reflected broader discourse patterns rather than isolated keywords. Second, analyzing which countries showed highest topic prevalence revealed geographic and economic patterns consistent with topic interpretations—mountain regions dominated the "mountain" topic while small island states showed high prevalence for sea-level rise themes. Third, testing topic correlations confirmed expected relationships: procedural topics positively correlated with each other while showing negative correlations with sectoral topics, validating the institutional-technical distinction emerging from qualitative interpretation.

The Control Index represents this study's primary methodological contribution, quantifying discourse concentration patterns that standard topic prevalence metrics cannot capture. While STM reveals what topics exist and how they vary across documents, it does not measure whether discourse is concentrated or distributed—a critical distinction for examining epistemological control. The index addresses this gap by measuring how much of each group's total discourse focuses on dominant topics versus distributing across the full thematic range.

The calculation proceeds in four steps. First, for each analytical category (income level, region, vulnerability type), the mean topic distribution is extracted across all documents in that group, creating a characteristic discourse profile. Second, the top three topics by prevalence are identified for each group, representing the dominant discourse themes. Third, the proportion of total discourse probability mass concentrated in these dominant topics is calculated, providing the raw dominance score. Fourth, this raw score is normalized against a uniform baseline where discourse distributes equally across all topics, producing a 0-1 scale where 0 represents perfect distribution and 1 represents complete concentration. This normalization ensures that values have consistent meaning regardless of the number of topics in the model, with a value of 0.5 representing 50% more concentration than expected under uniform distribution.

Establishing whether observed Control Index patterns reflected systematic institutional effects rather than random variation required formal hypothesis testing using STM's regression capabilities [@roberts2014]. The analysis tested three core theoretical claims about adaptation discourse. First, whether geographic vulnerability (SIDS, LLDC status) predicts discourse patterns more strongly than economic development level, which would suggest climate-responsive planning. Second, whether regional institutional networks create stronger convergence than shared climate challenges, indicating institutional rather than environmental drivers. Third, whether income level correlates with discourse autonomy, with higher-income countries showing greater diversity in adaptation approaches.

The estimateEffect function [@stm] estimated topic-covariate relationships through document-level regression, treating topic proportions as dependent variables and category membership as binary predictors. For each category within each grouping system, the analysis tested whether membership significantly predicted the prevalence of that category's dominant topics. The statistical model employed logistic-normal regression appropriate for proportional outcomes, with standard errors computed using the observed Fisher information matrix and significance assessed at α=0.05. Effect sizes were standardized to enable comparison across topics with different baseline prevalences, representing the proportional change in topic prevalence associated with category membership.

An important methodological consideration involves the aggregation of subcategory results to category-level estimates. To facilitate interpretation and comparison across the three categorization schemes, effect sizes from individual subcategories (e.g., each income level) were averaged to create category-level measures (e.g., overall income effect). This approach treats all subcategories equally regardless of sample size or internal variance, prioritizing interpretative clarity over statistical precision. While this simplification may mask heterogeneity within categories, it enables direct comparison of whether income, region, or geography most strongly influences adaptation discourse patterns.

The complete analytical pipeline was implemented in R [@base] with dependency management through renv [@renv] ensuring reproducibility. The STM package [@stm] provided core topic modeling functionality, with custom functions extending its capabilities for segmentation, aggregation, and the Control Index calculation. All code and processed data are available at https://github.com/khelfen/adaptation-knowledge, enabling both replication and adaptation of the Control Index methodology to other policy domains where questions of discourse concentration arise.
